idiom_name: createConfirmChannel + persistent publish + waitForConfirms + explicit ack
implementation_notes: The broker is the store; in Node the pattern is a short configuration protocol in amqplib: createConfirmChannel(), a durable (ideally quorum) queue, publish with { persistent: true, messageId } and await waitForConfirms() - RabbitMQ only confirms a persistent message once it has been persisted to a durable queue. On the consuming side use the consumer callback and call channel.ack(msg) after the business commit, channel.nack(msg, false, true) to requeue on a retryable failure; the messageId makes the inevitable duplicate suppressible downstream.
pitfalls: persistent: true on a non-durable queue, a transient exchange or a classic non-mirrored queue still loses messages at a broker restart.
waitForConfirms() rejects on a nack or a channel close - swallowing that rejection (or never awaiting it) turns the guarantee off while the code still looks right.
Acking before the business commit, or crashing between commit and ack, produces loss or duplicates respectively; both are the at-least-once contract, so the handler must be idempotent on messageId.
Unconfirmed publishes pile up in the client when the broker stalls; without awaiting confirms or backpressure the process runs out of memory instead of applying backpressure.

variants.name: KafkaJS transactional producer
variants.implementation_notes: Kafka's log is the store; KafkaJS exposes the broker transaction protocol as producer.transaction() with send/sendBatch, commit and abort, and transaction.sendOffsets() makes the consumer offset part of the same atomic unit. The required configuration is explicit: a stable transactionalId, idempotent: true and maxInFlightRequests: 1, which is exactly what guarantees exactly-once on the producer side after a retry. Choose it over an AMQP confirm channel when the sink is Kafka and atomicity across topics or between output and offsets matters.
pitfalls: Forgetting maxInFlightRequests: 1 or idempotent: true while declaring a transactionalId produces a producer that silently is not exactly-once.
An instance that dies mid-transaction blocks the transactionalId until the broker's transaction timeout expires; every commit/abort path must be wired or the producer stays stuck.
Consumers must use read_committed isolation, otherwise aborted records are still delivered.
The transactionalId must be stable per partition-owning instance: a random id per restart loses zombie fencing.
